title: Red Carpet for Xi, But Trade Truce Only Lasts a Few Months
summary:
President Xi Jinping of China arrived at the White House this week to a red carpet welcome from President Donald Trump. But behind the handshakes, Xi didn't get everything on his wish list.

China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower. Xi wants Washington to stay out of the way on trade, technology, and Taiwan. The two countries had been locked in a tit-for-tat tariff war — each side raising taxes on the other's goods. They agreed to pause that fight, but only from November to January. Xi had hoped for at least a year, hoping to ride out the rest of Trump's presidency. Instead, the toughest disputes — tariffs, rare earth supplies, and access to advanced US chips — are kicked into another round of negotiations.

Why does Xi need a deal? China's economy is struggling at home. The country sells record goods abroad, but Chinese consumers are holding back. Youth unemployment is stubbornly high, and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their homes. Trade is propping up growth, so access to overseas markets matters more than ever.

Taiwan remains the sharpest flashpoint. Xi has called US arms sales to Taiwan a red line. In May, he warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict." Trump then delayed a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, calling it a "very good negotiating chip." On Thursday, Xi repeated his hope that the US would oppose Taiwan independence. Trump has not publicly responded, and faces bipartisan pressure to keep supporting Taiwan.

The leaders also discussed artificial intelligence (AI). Xi said AI should always remain "under human control," but no concrete safeguards were announced. The talks ended with warm words — and plenty of unfinished business.
why_it_matters: A short tariff pause and the use of Taiwan arms as a 'negotiating chip' show how economic weakness and security threats are now tangled together in the world's most important relationship. The choices made now will shape which technologies, jobs and alliances the next generation inherits.

background_read: Xi Jinping (China's president and Communist Party leader since 2013) often speaks about restoring China's standing after what Chinese textbooks call the 'century of humiliation', when foreign powers forced unfair treaties on the country in the 1800s and early 1900s. That history explains why Beijing is so sensitive about being 'contained' by the United States.

Taiwan (a self-governing island that Beijing considers a breakaway province) remains the most dangerous issue in the relationship. Since 1979 the United States has formally recognised Beijing while still selling Taiwan defensive weapons under the Taiwan Relations Act, and every U.S. president since has had to balance those two commitments.

China's economy is the world's second largest, but it has slowed noticeably in recent years. Large property developers have run into severe trouble, leaving unfinished apartments and falling prices in a country where most families keep their savings in housing, while youth unemployment has stayed stubbornly high — which is why access to overseas markets matters so much to Beijing.

The United States has also restricted exports of advanced computer chips and the machines that make them, aiming to slow China's progress in artificial intelligence and advanced computing. That is one reason 'access to advanced US chips' is sitting on the negotiating table.
Rare earths (metals used in magnets, batteries and electronics) give China leverage in return, because it processes most of the global supply — a mirror image of America's strength in chips.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a pause is better than a spiral
perspectives.description: Even a two-month tariff pause gives businesses and exporters time to plan, and it keeps the two governments negotiating instead of escalating. From Washington's point of view, keeping rare earth supplies flowing and leaving the Taiwan arms package in reserve preserves leverage without provoking an immediate crisis.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — Xi left with little, and the risks remain
perspectives.description: Xi wanted a year-long pause to ride out the rest of Trump's presidency and got only November to January, while the hardest disputes were simply pushed into new talks. Meanwhile Washington's willingness to treat Taiwanese security as a bargaining chip alarms those who say a democracy's safety should not be traded away.

The tariff war described in the article follows a familiar pattern: each side raises costs on the other's goods, and both end up worse off. China's reliance on exports during a domestic slowdown and America's restrictions on advanced chips mean neither side can simply walk away — so rounds of talks replace resolutions.

Everything hinges on what happens when the pause expires: whether tariffs snap back, whether China's rare earth supply stays open, and whether any chip access is traded. Xi's call for AI to stay 'under human control' also sets up a future fight over rules for machines that neither country fully controls.
